summary: This standards-track memo defines a MIB module extending the Remote Monitoring MIB from RFC 2819. It describes managed objects used for real-time application quality of service monitoring.

eli5.summary: This is the list of gauges where quality reports for calls and apps get stored so a network manager can read them.

questions: what is a raqmon report collector
how does raqmon alarm on poor qos
subtitle: The SNMP MIB module where a RAQMON collector stores per-session quality reports and alarm thresholds.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications such as calls generate quality-of-service measurements, but a network manager needs a standard way to read them from the collector that receives the reports.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4711 defines the RAQMON MIB module, an extension of the RMON MIB, with three groups: raqmonSession (participant, QoS history and address tables), raqmonException (thresholds that trigger notifications) and raqmonConfig (collector settings).
tldr.outcome: RAQMON Report Collectors MUST implement the module, so management applications can read session quality over SNMP and be alerted when a session crosses a threshold.

today: RFC 4711 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Management Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module that extends the Remote Monitoring MIB of RFC 2819 with managed objects for real-time application quality-of-service (QoS) monitoring. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are defined with the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is written in SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The module sits in the RMON subtree: its module identity is { rmon 31 }, an allocation that follows RFC 3737.
sections.eli5: A MIB is a shared list of named gauges that a network manager can read. This one adds gauges for how well real-time apps are working.

sections.title: The RAQMON Framework
sections.content:
As outlined in RFC 4710, the framework has three entities: the RAQMON Data Source (RDS), the RAQMON Report Collector (RRC) and the RAQMON MIB structure. This MIB describes the information passed between report collectors and a RAQMON application, the management application that reads it.

The module MUST be implemented by RAQMON Report Collectors. A separate MIB module in RFC 4712 maps RAQMON PDUs onto an SNMP transport, and that module is normally implemented by data sources.
sections.eli5: Apps send small quality notes to a collector, like students handing reports to a teacher. This document describes the teacher's gradebook that a manager can look at.

sections.title: Session Tables
sections.content:
The raqmonSession group has three tables:

  • raqmonParticipantTable holds information about participants in active and closed sessions, aggregated since the session began. Each row is one session run by one participant, indexed by raqmonParticipantStartDate and raqmonParticipantIndex. Agents MUST NOT report identical start times for two sessions on the same host, and old inactive rows are removed when implementation-specific age or space limits are reached.
  • raqmonQosTable holds history: each entry comes from a single RAQMON packet and is indexed additionally by raqmonQosTime, in seconds from the start of the session.
  • raqmonParticipantAddrTable maps participant addresses to participant table indices, so applications can look up entries by address rather than by start date.

The participant table carries addresses, ports, payload types, setup delay, CPU and memory, round-trip time, jitter, one-way delay, packet and octet counts, losses and discards, plus a raqmonParticipantReportCaps bit set describing which items the participant can report. The QoS table holds a smaller set: end-to-end network delay in milliseconds, inter-arrival jitter in milliseconds, received and sent packets and octets, lost packets and a session status. A value of -1 means it was never reported.
sections.eli5: One logbook has a page per session with totals. Another has a line for every report during a session. A third is an index so you can find sessions by who was in them.

sections.title: Exceptions, Alarms and Configuration
sections.content:
The raqmonException group has a raqmonSessionExceptionTable of thresholds that trigger notifications for sessions with poor QoS. Each row holds a jitter threshold in milliseconds, a round-trip-time threshold in milliseconds and a lost-packets threshold in tenths of a percent (0 to 1000). A value during a session must be greater than or equal to the threshold for an exception to be created. Rows use a RowStatus and must have all read-create objects set before becoming active. The table MUST be persistent across agent reboots. When an entry fires, the collector sends the raqmonSessionAlarm notification, which includes the participant address and name, peer address, delay, jitter and packet counts.

The raqmonConfig group defines the collector's setup:

  • raqmonConfigPort: the UDP port to listen on for RAQMON reports on non-SNMP transports. If the transport is SNMP, writes have no effect because the standard port 162 is always used.
  • raqmonConfigPduTransport: which transports the collector supports (other, tcp, snmp).
  • raqmonConfigRaqmonPdus: a counter of RAQMON PDUs received.
  • raqmonConfigRDSTimeout: seconds without a PDU after which a session is considered terminated.
sections.eli5: You can set limits, such as how choppy a call may be. If a call is worse than a limit, the box rings an alarm for the manager. The box also has a few settings, like where to listen for reports.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Read-write objects can be sensitive. Setting raqmonRDSTimeout too low ends sessions too soon, and too high keeps ended sessions around and wastes memory. Wrong exception thresholds can flood management applications with notifications or hide real degradation, and a wrong raqmonConfigPort stops the collector from receiving PDUs.

Readable objects are sensitive too. The participant, QoS and participant address tables can reveal participant addresses and application traffic patterns, so even GET and NOTIFY access should be controlled and values possibly encrypted. The table structure also limits what View-based Access Control can do, because participant row indexes cannot be known in advance, and exception entries apply to all QoS table entries. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. IANA has no requirements; the root OID belongs to the RMON subtree reserved in RFC 3737.
sections.eli5: The gauges show who talked to whom, so only the right people should be allowed to read them. Wrong settings could also make the alarm ring too much or never.
